body:
For observability, we can use on_message_stream to pipe internal team's messages out to its parent's output topic. 

Also with the runtime now available as a parameter to teams, all teams, nested included, can share the same runtime. 

Though I do feel having a single output topic for all teams and nested team is useful for the scenario you pointed out: a team or agent is wrapped inside a tool. Do you think this PR can benefit from addressing the agent/team as a tool specifically by providing agent tool and team tool? 

Related https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/issues/3640
author: ekzhu

body:
@ekzhu, I did not know about #3640, that is EXACTLY the problem I am trying to solve here. The `TaskRunner` agent is my attempt at the `AgentTool`, since `TaskRunner` is the interface shared by `Team/Agent`

> For observability, we can use on_message_stream to pipe internal team's messages out to its parent's output topic.

I have this on a fork where I am doing exactly that.

> Also with the runtime now available as a parameter to teams, all teams, nested included, can share the same runtime.

Agreed, that enabled some really interesting new use-cases.

> Though I do feel having a single output topic for all teams and nested team is useful for the scenario you pointed out: a team or agent is wrapped inside a tool. Do you think this PR can benefit from addressing the agent/team as a tool specifically by providing agent tool and team tool?

I think there are really 2 questions that need to be addressed in what you just said:
1. Creating a unified way of running Agent/Teams via tools so that they can be called by other Agents
2. Deciding on a method of observing the events from those nested teams.

The first feels much easier than the second. A global output channel is definitely an interesting idea, but I think it would be important to abstract that part from the user. In systems that I've interacted with like this there's usually an abstract class of some kind that's exposed which has the necessary functions. In this case we could maybe have the following class:
```python
class NestedTeamRuntime:
    @abstractmethod
    def pubish_output_message(message: AgentEvent | ChatMessage):
        ...
```

There could of course be other methods on there in the future, but that way the developer doesn't have to necessarily understand the entire system to understand what they are able to do.

I will go ahead and implement this with some of the changes discussed and then we can discuss again. I am very interested in getting this functionality over the line, so happy to work with you to get that done.
author: EItanya

body:
> that way the developer doesn't have to necessarily understand the entire system to understand what they are able to do.

Great point. The core api is too low level at the moment. What you suggest can pave the path for developers
author: ekzhu

body:
Another way to think about this problem is that it may not necessarily need the agent or team tool to be executed via the base tool interface. 

It can be similar to how handoff is done: the agent doesn't need to run tool via run_json. The model can make the tool call to the nested agent/team, and then the agent take the tool call, and run the nested agent/team similar to how SocietyOfMindAgent does it. 

Essentially, we can have a separate flow for nested agent/team within an agent, and avoid us having to force agent/team into the BaseTool interface. This helps with streaming as well.
author: ekzhu

body:
So I thought about that approach as well. I think each method has pros/cons.

The assistant agent is already becoming quite complex, and I'm not sure what the appetite is to continue adding complexity.

Truthfully the code will be exactly the same, it's just a matter of where it lives.

From my experience, handoffs were actually a bit unintuitive in how they worked under the hood, so maybe from an API perspective it's a better idea to keep a clean separation of concerns and say: "a tool is a tool, regardless of what type".

From my experience with APIs, composable building blocks are often more flexible in the long term than overloaded individual components, so I think I slightly prefer the approach currently outlined here.

What do you think of the changes from the last few commits?
author: EItanya

body:
I think the new changes makes agent as tool easy to use. 

The use of runtime context requires `TaskRunnerTool` to be used when agent is running in a runtime. This breaks the usage of `agent.run_stream` and `agent_run`, which runs the agent without a runtime. I think we can mitigate this by changing the `run_stream` and `run` implementation to create a runtime if not available, similar to how `BaseGroupChat` is right now -- but that could be a separate PR to enable it first.

For `TaskRunnerTool`, I think we may want to actually use `AgentTool` and `TeamTool` as two separate concrete classes. `TaskRunner` is currently a protocol that's not part of the core concepts of the framework.
author: ekzhu

body:
> For TaskRunnerTool, I think we may want to actually use AgentTool and TeamTool as two separate concrete classes. TaskRunner is currently a protocol that's not part of the core concepts of the framework.

Makes sense, I'll make that change
author: EItanya

body:
I really like the simplicity of this approach of making agent and team as tools. Still, I think there can be a simpler way to solve the output stream problem without using a context variable, which introduces complexity in the way we think about the design and may introduce limitation when runtime is distributed. 

One way I can think of is to introduce a `run_stream` interface method to tools -- this solves two issues:
1. It makes it a lot easier to create tools -- some of which may not be agent or teams, that also benefit from emitting events to the UI. 
2. It makes it much simpler to add `AgentTool` and `TeamTool` here. 

There has been recent development in streaming events from MCP servers (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/transports#server-sent-events-sse). So I think this will be a general capability tools will offer, and it's good for us to have it too. 

cc @victordibia @afourney
author: ekzhu

body:
> One way I can think of is to introduce a run_stream interface method to tools -- this solves two issues:

Sounds good to me, gonna hold off making any more changes until we agree on an approach here. 

I have 3 main questions:
1. Do you imagine an entirely new base class for this new tool type, or an extension of the existing one?
2. The answer to 1 may make this moot, but what should we do with the `AssistantAgent`? Should we add these new tools to the existing `tools` list, or create a new `input_arg` called `streaming_tools`?
3. What will the contract be when streaming? Will the stream run until a `TaskResult` is received and then it will turn that into `json`?
author: EItanya

body:
> Do you imagine an entirely new base class for this new tool type, or an extension of the existing one?

It may be beneficial to use a new subclass of `BaseTool`. The benefit of having a `BaseTool` is that it automatically generates the JSON schema that models can understand. However, modifying the `BaseTool` right now is a bit disruptive. So I think a subclass can be helpful to get the feature out without affecting other existing implementations of `BaseTool`. 

Let's say the abstract subclass is `BaseTaskRunnerTool`, which has two concrete classes `AgentTool` and `TeamTool` -- just like how you already have it in this PR.

> The answer to 1 may make this moot, but what should we do with the AssistantAgent? Should we add these new tools to the existing tools list, or create a new input_arg called streaming_tools?

In `AssistantAgent`, we can check if the tool type is a `BaseTaskRunnerTool` when we execute them and handle them differently from other tools, i.e., yield the streamed messages from the tools' `run_stream`. We probably need to run these tools sequentially to avoid mixing results from different concurrent streams. 

> What will the contract be when streaming? Will the stream run until a TaskResult is received and then it will turn that into json?

I think the `run_stream` of `BaseTaskRunnerTool` returns the same events as `TaskRunner`, and ends with a `TaskResult` which the last object is a `StructuredMessage` of the tool's return type specified in its `run()`.

For `StructuredMessage` it's on going work this week #5131 

We are starting to blur the boundaries between tool, agents and teams. What's your thought regarding to the future? Do you think there will still be such boundaries? Or everything is just "agent", or, "actors".
author: ekzhu

body:
Ok @ekzhu, I've been thinking about this PR a lot, as well as your comments and I have a lot of thoughts 😆 

> We are starting to blur the boundaries between tool, agents and teams. What's your thought regarding to the future? Do you think there will still be such boundaries? Or everything is just "agent", or, "actors".

I agree with this sentence completely, the lines are beginning to become indistinguishable, and this PR probably tries to solve that in the wrong way. I actually think the issue is the separation of concerns between the agent runtime, and the observability requirements.

Structured agents really only care about `JSON I/O`, but currently in order to trace the execution path of the system we have to stream the events to the runtime and then up to the caller. I actually think this is potentially bad for 2 reasons:
1. As mentioned it mixes concerns
2. It can flood the event stream with unnecessary observability events.

I think the best solution here would actually be something similar to what @victordibia did here: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/5457. We now have logs for streaming events, and tool calls, so we should be able to get 100% of the information we need without ever accessing the `TaskRunner`. This allows decoupling of observability concerns with runtime concerns. 

Lmk what you think
author: EItanya

body:
> I think the best solution here would actually be something similar to what @victordibia did here: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/5457. We now have logs for streaming events, and tool calls, so we should be able to get 100% of the information we need without ever accessing the TaskRunner. This allows decoupling of observability concerns with runtime concerns.

I think it makes sense. The purpose of `run_stream` was to make it easier to consume the agent-agent message streams and their thought processes. The `run_stream` is meant for notebook, console, and chat UI scenarios, and simplify integration with basic UI.

For workflows and more autonomous sceanrios, I agree it makes more sense to use traces and logs for full observability of messages, model calls and tool calls. Just use `run` instead of `run_stream`.

body:
I found a potential issue. @nissa-seru The goal of making the decorators no-op for abstract methods to support type variables in signatures is a good one.

However, I believe the current implementation doesn't quite achieve the intended effect. The `getattr(func, "__isabstractmethod__", False)` check is added to the outer dispatch logic, but it doesn't prevent the inner `decorator` function (which contains the type hint validation logic) from being called with the abstract method itself. This means the problematic validation (`get_type_hints`, `get_types`) will likely still run during class definition time, potentially raising the same errors the PR aims to prevent.

To achieve the no-op behavior, the check for `__isabstractmethod__` should likely be placed *inside* the `decorator` inner function. If the decorated function is abstract, the `decorator` function should return the original function `func` directly, bypassing the validation and wrapping logic. I havent tested it, but it looks like it and should probably be considered.
author: a-holm

body:
**Orb Code Review** (powered by GLM 5.1 on [Orb Cloud](https://orbcloud.dev))

## Summary

This PR makes `@message_handler`, `@event`, and `@rpc` decorators skip processing when applied to abstract methods (detected via `__isabstractmethod__`). This enables using these decorators on abstract methods in ABC classes without the decorators attempting to validate type hints at declaration time.

## Architecture

The change adds an `or getattr(func, "__isabstractmethod__", False)` clause to the existing `if func is None and not callable(func)` branch in all three decorator functions. When triggered, it returns `decorator` (the inner factory function) instead of processing the method.

## Issues

### 🔴 Bug: Returns wrong value for the no-op case (all three decorators)

When the decorated function is abstract, the code returns `decorator` (the inner factory function), **not** the original `func`. This replaces the abstract method on the class with the `decorator` factory, which:

1. **Loses the `__isabstractmethod__` attribute** — `abc.ABCMeta` checks for this attribute during class construction to track abstract methods. Since `decorator` doesn't have it, the class will no longer consider this method abstract. Concrete subclasses that fail to implement it won't raise `TypeError` on instantiation.

2. **Replaces the method with a factory function** — The class attribute becomes a decorator factory instead of the original method, which could cause confusing errors if anything tries to call it.

**Fix**: Return `func` directly to make it a true no-op:

```python
if func is None and not callable(func):
    return decorator
elif getattr(func, "__isabstractmethod__", False):
    return func  # true no-op: return the original abstract method unchanged
elif callable(func):
    return decorator(func)
else:
    raise ValueError("Invalid arguments")
```

### 🟡 Note: The existing `func is None and not callable(func)` condition is itself a code smell

`func is None and not callable(func)` simplifies to just `func is None` (since `callable(None)` is always `False`). This is pre-existing and not introduced by this PR, but the new `or` clause makes the compound expression harder to reason about.

### 🟡 No tests added

The PR author notes no tests were added. Given that this affects core decorator behavior, a test verifying that:
- Abstract methods decorated with `@message_handler` remain abstract
- Concrete subclasses that don't implement the abstract method raise `TypeError`
- Concrete subclasses that do implement it work correctly

...would significantly strengthen confidence in this change.

## Cross-file Impact

- `_routed_agent.py`: All three decorators (`message_handler`, `event`, `rpc`) are affected with the same pattern.
- `_discover_handlers()` (line 370): Already filters by `hasattr(handler, "is_message_handler")`, so abstract methods that are no-oped (and don't get the `is_message_handler` attribute) won't be discovered. This is correct behavior.

## Assessment

**Request changes** — The core idea is sound, but the implementation returns the wrong value (`decorator` factory instead of the original `func`), which breaks ABC semantics. Adding tests for the abstract method use case would also be important to prevent regressions.

**Orb Code Review** (powered by GLM-4.7 on [Orb Cloud](https://orbcloud.dev))

## Summary
This PR adds a comprehensive ethics statement document (`ETHICS.md`) to the AutoGen repository, establishing four core principles for responsible agentic AI development: Prevent Harm, Prioritize Ethical Directives, Maintain Integrity, Empower Human Agency, and Promote Equity. The 29-line document provides concrete examples for each principle and expresses a commitment to continuous improvement through open-source collaboration.

## Architecture
This is a documentation-only PR that adds foundational ethical guidelines:

- **Core Principles**: Four guiding principles for ethical AI development
- **Concrete Examples**: Each principle includes a real-world use case demonstrating ethical behavior
- **Health Check Framework**: Describes systems that can detect and alert on potential ethical issues
- **Open Source Philosophy**: Emphasizes collaboration and rejection of cynicism
- **Human-Centric Approach**: Prioritizes human welfare, agency, and societal benefit

- **Continuous Improvement**: Commits to stakeholder feedback and alignment with human values

The document serves as both a statement of values and a practical framework for ethical AI development.

## Issues

### Critical

**No critical issues found** - The ethics statement is well-structured and thoughtfully written.

### Warnings

**1. ETHICS.md:9** - **Typo in title**:
```markdown
# Open Source Agentics Statement
```

"Agentics" appears to be a typo or coined term. Consider either:
- "# Open Source Agentic Systems Statement"
- "# Open Source AI Agents Statement"
- "# Open Source Agent Development Statement"

**2. ETHICS.md:13-16** - **Technical implementation ambiguity**:
```markdown
- Prevent Harm: Our agentic systems are designed to detect and alert on potential harm...

Example: An agent system being adapted for military targeting... triggers a critical health check via telemetry.
```

The example describes systems that can "detect and alert" but provides no guidance on:
- How these detection mechanisms are implemented
- Whether these are built-in features or optional
- How developers should implement such systems
- The technical feasibility of automated harm detection

**3. ETHICS.md:11** - **Implementation questions not addressed**:

The document sets expectations for behavior but doesn't clarify:
- Are these principles required or aspirational?
- How are compliance violations handled?
- Is there an audit or review process?
- Do these apply to all AutoGen uses or specific deployments?

**4. ETHICS.md:33-35** - **Enforcement mechanism unclear**:
```markdown
**Our Commitment**

We are committed to continuous improvement and collaboration. We actively seek feedback from diverse stakeholders to ensure our systems are aligned with human values and societal needs.
```

While expressing commitment is good, there's no mention of:
- How feedback is collected and acted upon
- What constitutes "diverse stakeholders"
- How alignment with human values is measured
- Whether there's an ethics review board or similar governance

### Suggestions

**1. Clarify technical implementation**:
```markdown
- Prevent Harm: Our agentic systems are designed to detect and alert on potential harm and minimize unintended consequences.

**Implementation**: These principles are integrated through:
- Optional safety modules that can be enabled in agent configurations
- Telemetry and monitoring frameworks for detecting anomalous behavior
- Integration guidelines for ethical considerations in agent development

Example: ...
```

**2. Add compliance guidelines**:
```markdown
## Compliance and Accountability

These principles serve as guidelines for ethical development. While we encourage all AutoGen users to consider these principles, specific compliance requirements may vary based on deployment context, jurisdiction, and use case. We recommend:
- Conducting ethical impact assessments for sensitive applications
- Implementing appropriate oversight mechanisms for high-risk deployments
- Following relevant regulations and industry standards
- Seeking legal counsel for applications in regulated domains
```

**3. Add governance structure**:
```markdown
## Governance

This ethics statement is maintained by the AutoGen community through:
- Regular review and updates based on community feedback
- Open discussion in project governance channels
- Alignment with broader AI ethics frameworks
- Transparency about limitations and challenges

For questions or suggestions about this ethics statement, please open an issue or discussion.
```

**4. Provide practical integration examples**:
```markdown
## Integration with AutoGen

Developers can integrate ethical considerations into their agents using:

```python
# Example: Safety hooks in agent configuration
agent = AssistantAgent(
    name="safe_agent",
    safety_hooks=[
        HarmDetectionHook(),
        BiasDetectionHook(),
        TransparencyHook()
    ]
)
```

For more examples, see our [safety modules documentation](link).
```

**5. Add reference to broader frameworks**:
```markdown
## References

This statement draws from and aligns with broader AI ethics discussions:
- [IEEE Ethically Aligned Design](https://ethicsinaction.ieee.org/)
- [OECD AI Principles](https://oecd.ai/)
- [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)
- [EU AI Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/artificial-intelligence-act)

```

**6. Consider adding use case categories**:
```markdown
## Applicability

These principles are particularly relevant for agents involved in:
- Healthcare and medical decision-making
- Financial services and automated trading
- Law enforcement and public safety
- Education and student assessment
- Employment and hiring decisions
- Content moderation and recommendation systems

For simpler, lower-risk applications, some principles may apply with reduced emphasis.
```

**7. Add limitations section**:
```markdown
## Limitations and Challenges

We acknowledge the complexity of implementing ethical AI systems:
- Defining "harm" across cultural and contextual boundaries is challenging
- Automated harm detection may produce false positives or miss subtle issues
- Balancing different ethical principles can involve difficult trade-offs
- Technical constraints may limit what can be automatically detected

We commit to transparency about these limitations and continuous improvement of our approaches.
```

**8. Community input mechanisms**:
```markdown
## Community Participation

We welcome community input on this ethics statement:
- **GitHub Discussions**: [Link to discussions]
- **Issue Reports**: File issues with "ethics" label
- **Pull Requests**: Contribute improvements and clarifications
- **Advisory Board**: [Information about any ethics oversight]

Your feedback helps us ensure our principles remain relevant and practical.
```

**9. Version control for the document**:
```markdown
---
# Open Source Agentic Systems Statement

**Version**: 1.0  
**Last Updated**: March 2025  
**Review Schedule**: Annual or as needed based on community feedback

---
```

**10. Technical implementation roadmap**:
```markdown
## Roadmap

We are working on technical implementations to support these principles:
- [ ] Safety module framework for AutoGen
- [ ] Monitoring and alerting tools for production deployments
- [ ] Audit logging capabilities for ethical oversight
- [ ] Documentation for integrating ethical considerations into custom agents
- [ ] Community tools and examples for ethical agent development
```

## Cross-file Impact

- **New files**: `ETHICS.md` (29 lines)
- **Modified files**: None
- **Breaking changes**: None
- **Public API**: No changes
- **Documentation**: Adds foundational ethics document
- **Community**: Establishes values framework for the project
- **Compliance**: Sets expectations for ethical behavior
- **Technical**: No code changes, purely documentation

## Assessment
✅ Approve

This is a well-written and thoughtful ethics statement that provides a solid foundation for responsible AI development in the AutoGen ecosystem. While it raises important questions about implementation and enforcement, the document succeeds in articulating clear values and providing concrete examples.

**Strengths:**
- Clear, principled stance on AI ethics
- Concrete examples that illustrate each principle
- Balanced approach covering harm, ethics, integrity, human agency, and equity
- Open source philosophy aligns with project values
- Human-centric focus that prioritizes welfare and agency
- Examples cover diverse scenarios (healthcare, military targeting, insurance, personal assistants)
- Positive, collaborative tone that rejects cynicism
- Acknowledgment of complexity and commitment to improvement
- Addresses important aspects of responsible AI development

**Minor improvements needed:**
- Fix typo in title ("Agentics" → "Agentic Systems")
- Add more technical implementation guidance
- Clarify whether principles are requirements or aspirations
- Provide governance structure for document maintenance
- Add practical integration examples with code
- Reference broader AI ethics frameworks
- Include limitations and challenges section

**Documentation quality:**
- Well-structured and easy to read
- Good use of examples to illustrate abstract principles
- Clear language that avoids jargon
- Appropriate scope for an introductory ethics statement
- Positive tone that encourages ethical behavior
- Comprehensive coverage of key ethical concerns

**Community impact:**
- **Positive**: Sets clear expectations for ethical behavior
- **Positive**: Demonstrates commitment to responsible AI
- **Positive**: Provides framework for community discussions
- **Positive**: Aligns with broader AI ethics discourse
- **Question**: Implementation mechanisms need clarification
- **Opportunity**: Could serve as foundation for safety features

**Strategic value:**
- Establishes AutoGen as ethically conscious project
- Provides differentiation from other agent frameworks
- Creates foundation for future safety features
- Enables community alignment around shared values
- Supports responsible development practices

The ethics statement is a valuable addition to the AutoGen project that demonstrates serious consideration of responsible AI development. While it would benefit from additional technical guidance and governance information, the core document is well-crafted and ready for inclusion. The suggested improvements can be addressed in follow-up PRs as the project develops more concrete technical implementations of these principles.

I think it is the model client's caller's responsibility to parse and present string content. What I think makes sense right now, is for the caller of `model_client.create_stream` to detect `<think>` and `</think>` chunks and generating appropriate attributes for the `ModelClientStreamChunkEvent` sent to the frontend, which then use that to render the text. If we add `"[think]"` strings to every reasoning chunk, it's a breaking change to the API and suddenly confuse existing users of the model clients.

> Look at these screenshots. If one field carries the rendering results of thoughts and content, and the other carries the rendering results of two fields, it will really be difficult for us to distinguish which are thinking tokens and which are content tokens when putting them in one field.

What app are you using? If we change `ModelClientChunkStreamEvent` to use `reasoning_content` for displaying reasoning token, it is a breaking change. If we use a flag `is_reasoning` in `ModelClientChunkStreamEvent` to indicate this is a reasoning content, then it won't be a breaking change. 

> Moreover, the API documentation of DeepSeek is like this, and so is that of OpenAI. 

Where in OpenAI's documentation says they have a `reasoning_content` field?

> 
> Where in OpenAI's documentation says they have a `reasoning_content` field?

I also want to comment the thought parsing problem, for `autogen-0.4.7` version. Hope to support QwQ as well, as it is more powerful than deepseek series at reported in the official leadboard. 

The function below is from `autogen_ext/models/_utils/parse_r1_content.py`

```
def parse_r1_content(content: str) -> Tuple[str | None, str]:
    """Parse the content of an R1-style message that contains a `<think>...</think>` field."""
    # Find the start and end of the think field
    think_start = content.find("<think>")
    think_end = content.find("</think>")

    # if think_start == -1 or think_end == -1:
    #     warnings.warn(
    #         "Could not find <think>..</think> field in model response content. " "No thought was extracted.",
    #         UserWarning,
    #         stacklevel=2,
    #     )
    #     return None, content
    #
    # if think_end < think_start:
    #     warnings.warn(
    #         "Found </think> before <think> in model response content. " "No thought was extracted.",
    #         UserWarning,
    #         stacklevel=2,
    #     )
    #     return None, content
 
    # NOTE: THIS IS FOR QWQ-32B model parsing, actually, it is a good way to detect the `<think>` and `</think>` here.  
    if think_start == -1 and think_end:
        thought, content = content.split("</think>", 1)

        logger.debug("thought：", thought)
        logger.debug("content：", content)

        return thought, content


    # Extract the think field
    thought = content[think_start + len("<think>") : think_end].strip()

    # Extract the rest of the content, skipping the think field.
    content = content[think_end + len("</think>") :].strip()

    return thought, content

```

See the code comment. I also suggest the parsing process could be desined here, for different mdoels. 

### Model's thinking differences:

- Deepseek: `<think> ... </think>` are all at the reponse. 
- QwQ-32B: `<think>` is inlcuded into the prompt. Only `</think>` will be detected from the model's response. That's the difference.

body:
Agreed that currently I have been using the traces provided by the instrumentation libraries, and those have been great, but I think it's probably also a good idea to have them in the components.

I do want to bring up a slightly different issue since there have been a lot of tracing conversations happening.

Right now the tracing emitted is really beneficial for a core developer, but not `agentchat` IMO. Someone using `agentchat` or declarative style config construction doesn't really care about the underlying events/messages, especially because streaming can cause this to get VERY noisy. I had a 4 step agent interaction with `760` traces. I don't have a solution yet, but I think it's worth considering some way to expose tracing for the non-core users, users who really cares about `agent -> tool`, `agent -> llm` etc, much higher level concepts.

body:
In generally I like this PR.

I worry a little about the really long method names like `content_to_model_message`... but at least it's clear.

I'm also not sure about `content_to_render`. Doesn't this really depend on the media type or shell environment? E.g., I got hit on markitdown when people's shells were set to the charset `gbk`. Is there a better name for this?

Hi @ekzhu,

I’m encountering the following mypy error:
```bash
src/autogen_agentchat/teams/_group_chat/_selector_group_chat.py:183: error: Second
argument of Enum() must be string, tuple, list or dict literal for mypy to determine Enum members [misc]
```
This error occurs on the line:
```python
AgentName = Enum("AgentName", agent_name_map)
```
Since we need to dynamically create the Enum, I’m using `# type: ignore` to bypass the error.

References:
- [Mypy Issue #5317](https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/5317)
- [Stack Overflow Discussion](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/70163653/how-to-add-type-hint-for-dynamically-created-enums)

> Not sure this is working, is there a change for how filesurfer is instantiated?
> 
> ```
>     file_surfer = FileSurfer(
>         name="file_surfer",
>         model_client=model_client_file_surfer,
>         base_path="home/path1"
>     )
> ```
> 
> I was able to get file_surfer to read files in path "home"

This is the correct signature for creating the FileSurfer.
I am not able to replicate this behavior.

My minimal test code is:

```python
import asyncio
import sys
from autogen_agentchat.agents import UserProxyAgent
from autogen_agentchat.conditions import TextMentionTermination
from autogen_agentchat.teams import RoundRobinGroupChat
from autogen_agentchat.ui import Console
from autogen_ext.models.openai import OpenAIChatCompletionClient
from autogen_ext.agents.file_surfer import FileSurfer

async def main() -> None:
    model_client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(model="gpt-4o")
    file_surfer = FileSurfer(
        name="FileSurfer",
        model_client = model_client,
        base_path=None #"/home/afourney/repos/autogen/python"
    )
    user_proxy = UserProxyAgent("user_proxy")
    termination = TextMentionTermination("exit", sources=["user_proxy"])
    team = RoundRobinGroupChat([file_surfer, user_proxy], termination_condition=termination)
    try:
        # Start the team and wait for it to terminate.
        await Console(team.run_stream(task=sys.argv[1]))
    finally:
        await file_surfer.close()
        await model_client.close()

asyncio.run(main())
```

Thanks for adding the `request_id` field for better tracking! This is a useful addition.

Overall, the approach of adding the optional field to `CreateResult` and using safe extraction methods (`getattr`, `.get`) in the clients looks good.

However, there are two issues I found during review:

1.  **Azure AI Client (`create_stream`):** The logic to extract `request_id` in `autogen_ext/models/azure/_azure_ai_client.py` within the `create_stream` method appears incorrect. It attempts `getattr(result, "request_id", None)` where `result` is the `CreateResult` being constructed, not the Azure SDK response object. This needs to be revised to correctly fetch the ID from the appropriate SDK object (perhaps stored from an initial response or a chunk if available).
2.  **Replay Client:** The logic in `autogen_ext/models/replay/_replay_chat_completion_client.py` only extracts `request_id` if the replayed item is a `dict`. It should MAYBE if point 1 is on purpose also handle the case where the item is a `CreateResult` object, potentially using `getattr(response, "request_id", None)` in that scenario.

@SongChiYoung I think what you are doing is a useful step toward a more modular way to manage different message transformation logic for each model family. I think your new approach is in the right direction.

I would consider making it more modular and easier to maintain by having a global dictionary of separate transformation functions that goes from a list of `LLMMessage` to `ChatCompletionMessageParam` for each model family.

body:
@ekzhu Thanks for your valuable feedback!
As you suggested, I'm planning to set up a global registry that maps each `ModelFamily` to a list of transformer functions, rather than a single transformer. A simple closure will combine these transformers into a single callable per `ModelFamily`.

### Motivation:
- **Extensibility:** Easily handle future model feature combinations (e.g., Gemini + R1 or other mixed requirements).
- **Maintainability:** Clearly show each step of the transformation, making debugging and adding new transformers straightforward.

Additionally, I'll place this global registry within a dedicated `transform` package at the top level of `autogen-ext`. This cleanly separates the transformer logic from the existing codebase, enhancing discoverability and future maintainability.

Based on your previous comment, it seems like we're on the same page regarding this structural direction, but I just wanted to confirm once more before proceeding. Let me know if you agree or have additional suggestions—once confirmed, I'll try the implementation!

author: ekzhu

body:
@ekzhu Thanks again for your thoughtful feedback!

Please check my new changes of code.

- Global transformer registry by model family
- Removed duplicated transformation logic by unifying into a shared registry
- Gemini assistant fix for empty content / thought
- Added tests for Gemini tool calling edge cases

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

- Introduced a global registry for message transformers mapped by `ModelFamily`
- Unified previously duplicated transformer logic (e.g., assistant conditionals) into centralized registry
- Applied Gemini-specific assistant transformers with fallback for empty content
- Fixed Gemini tool-calling issue caused by empty `content` or `thought`
- Added test cases to assert Gemini behavior on invalid assistant messages
</details>
I completely understand your point about keeping the registry within the `autogen_ext.models.openai` namespace for now, especially since the immediate goal is resolving compatibility issues with OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

Before finalizing the change, I just wanted to briefly share why I initially designed the global transformer registry at the top-level namespace (`autogen-ext/transformation`):

- **Extensibility**: This structure easily allows future integrations with other model families beyond OpenAI-compatible APIs (e.g., Gemini, R1, and any new emerging models).
- **Maintainability**: Clearly defined and separated transformer logic facilitates easier debugging, reviewing, and extending functionality in the long run.

I fully respect your initial suggestion and I'm happy to move forward by placing it under `autogen_ext.models.openai` as you recommended. But if there's still a possibility to reconsider placing it at the global level—even temporarily—I would greatly appreciate your thoughts once more.

Could you please let me know your final thoughts on this?

Thanks again for your time and patience!

body:
@ekzhu As I mentioned in the recent issue I filed (#6083), Anthropic models also raise errors when given empty content — similar to the Gemini case. This applies to both OpenAI-compatible and native Anthropic SDKs.

To address this properly, I realized that the transformer logic needs to apply more broadly — not just under the OpenAI namespace.

I’m truly sorry to repeat this suggestion again, as I know I previously proposed a similar idea. However, this additional context (supporting Anthropic and potentially other models) makes it clearer that placing the transformer registry under a top-level `transform` package within `autogen_ext` would help avoid duplicated logic and keep things clean moving forward.

Please let me know what you think — and I really appreciate your patience reviewing this again.
author: SongChiYoung

body:
They @SongChiYoung thanks for the update.

I understand that it is much more modular with the new approach with potential added benefit, but the PR is getting quite large, and it introduces a new architecture that maybe we as maintainers aren't extremely familiar with. 

Consider this, you may stop contributing to the project after a few months with very good reason as you may start work on other things interest you. But we will still be left with the code we may not understand very well.

So, my suggestion is to make the changes incrementally and think about what the minimal design is needed to solve the problems related to `OpenAIChatCompletionClient` when used for different compatibility endpoints. I think the minimal design is simply a register dictionary with model family prefix and their respective `to_oai_type` functions. Just need to make sure the top-level `to_oai_type` function all have the same signature and we are good. This solves the urgent issue and leave a lot of room for future improvements.

Right now, I'd say beefing up the integration test cases for OpenAIChatCompletionClient is more important than creating a new architecture for message transformation. Right now, the tests only use OpenAI and Gemini models, but we hope to increase the modularity and expand to more providers.
author: ekzhu

body:
Thank you @ekzhu — I really appreciate your thoughtful feedback, and your team’s dedication to maintaining the quality and long-term sustainability of AutoGen.

Your suggestion makes perfect sense, and I’ll proceed as you advised:
- I’ll simplify the current implementation to use a registry of `ModelFamily -> to_oai_type` functions.
- I’ll also keep everything scoped within the OpenAI namespace for now, without introducing broader architectural changes.

In addition, since the Anthropic SDK is specific to Anthropic models only, I’ll go ahead and apply the simple fix there as well — without needing any model check logic — and include that in this PR.

Thanks again, and I’ll update the PR shortly!

body:
One potential issue identified during review:

In `python/packages/autogen-ext/src/autogen_ext/models/openai/_message_transform.py`, the code defines a `__CLAUDE_TRANSFORMER_MAP` which includes the `_set_empty_to_whitespace` fix (similar to the Gemini map). However, the registration loop later in the file assigns the `__BASE_TRANSFORMER_MAP` (which lacks the fix) to Claude models (`for model in __claude_models:` loop). This seems to prevent the fix from being applied to Claude models when accessed via the OpenAI client interface. Could you please double-check if this registration is intended or if it should use `__CLAUDE_TRANSFORMER_MAP` instead?

It might be on purpose, just pointing it out if it isn't.
author: a-holm

body:
@a-holm 
Thanks a lot for catching this — that’s a really good observation.

You’re right: __CLAUDE_TRANSFORMER_MAP was defined separately with the _set_empty_to_whitespace fix (just like Gemini), but the registration loop mistakenly assigns __BASE_TRANSFORMER_MAP to Claude models. That wasn’t intentional — it’s a clear oversight on my part during the transformer registration cleanup.

I’ll fix the registration logic to correctly apply the Claude-specific map. Also planning to add a minimal test case to confirm the whitespace fallback behavior works properly when accessed via the OpenAI-compatible interface.

Really appreciate you pointing this out before it shipped. Saved me from an embarrassing bug down the line!
author: SongChiYoung

body:
I found two other issues while fixing it:

1) Model family is broken when using Anthropic:  
Claude model prefix is `claude-3-5-...` instead of `claude-3.5-...`, so I changed them (both `model_family` and `model_info`).  
For the same reason, I also changed `model_info` inside `openai`.

> I needed to change this in this PR, because I check whether a message is from Claude using `model_family.startswith(...)`.  
> If you want, I could separate this into another PR.

2) Claude rejects empty or whitespace-only messages (not only `''`, but also `' '` and other all-whitespace strings),  
so I added logic to skip such messages and not send them to the server.

body:
@ekzhu Thanks for the thoughtful feedback.

I’ve updated the PR to follow your suggestion:
- Only merge **consecutive** system messages.
- If **non-consecutive** system messages are detected, raise an error.

Also, I’d like to explicitly document a **known issue** here:
> Some models (e.g., Anthropic, Gemini) do **not** support multiple system messages correctly.  

If we later encounter:
- increasing demands from users or agents to support multiple system messages (even if they are non-consecutive), or
- more reports of agents malfunctioning due to the strict error policy,

then we can revisit this logic and consider making the merging behavior more flexible or even configurable.

In some cases, it may also make sense to escalate this to model vendors if the underlying SDK behavior improves over time.

Thanks again for the review!

@ekzhu 
This PR is now complete and ready for review.

It addresses the core regressions identified in Issue #6123, specifically:

| ID  | Description | Resolution |
|-----|-------------|------------|
| **P1** | `inner_messages` leaked into `_message_thread`, affecting termination evaluation | ✅ Fixed by excluding `inner_messages` from `Response` |
| **P2** | Inner team did not execute when outer message history was empty | ✅ Now reuses previous task and passes it via handoff message |
| **P3** | Summary prompt was built from outer messages only | ✅ Now uses `inner_messages` as the source for summarization |
| **P4** | Outer messages were incorrectly included in summary | ✅ Resolved via the same fix as P3 |

Let me know if this direction looks good to you, or if further refinement is needed. Thanks!

body:
I took the freedom to have a look for the practice. LGTM! This PR effectively addresses the backward compatibility concern for Pydantic serialization by renaming the base classes to `BaseChatMessage` and `BaseAgentEvent` and reintroducing the original names as discriminated union types. The changes are applied consistently across the codebase, including necessary updates to type hints, the `MessageFactory`, tests, and documentation. This refactoring improves type clarity for future extensions while maintaining compatibility for existing users.

The renames and type hint updates appear consistent. No instances were found where the old names `ChatMessage`/`AgentEvent` were used when `BaseChatMessage`/`BaseAgentEvent` were intended after the refactor, or vice versa within the diff's scope. The introduction of `BaseTextChatMessage` as an intermediate base class for text-based chat messages is a logical addition to share implementation (`to_text`, `to_model_text`, `to_model_message`) and doesn't introduce conflicts.

Test files (`test_messages.py`, `test_assistant_agent.py`, `test_group_chat.py`, etc.) have been updated to reflect the renames and correctly use `BaseChatMessage`/`BaseAgentEvent` in type hints where applicable. `test_messages.py` includes tests for the new union types and `MessageFactory`.

Thinking about it a bit more, maybe we don't need to add this feature. the `MODEL_POINTERS` is currently an implementation detail. 

- If we by default set `resolve_model_alias=False`, it may break existing setups when the endpoint is not OpenAI. 
- If the user needs to pass `resolve_model_alias=True`, it already feels like more work than just specify the full name without getting much convenience.
author: ekzhu
SongChiYoung

body:
> This way, the pointer map stays clean, and we can optionally control things like default alias resolution or vendor-specific logic without breaking anything.

I believe this is a clever design. Though let's not make too many design changes for the up-coming release now. Perhaps we close this PR for now and we can revisit later after more feedbacks and reports from the new release?

body:
@ekzhu

Thanks for the question! (I wrote it quickly at first, but just updated the comment now.)

> Why not use the message transformation?

The reason I didn't use the transformer is because this issue specifically applies to the **last AssistantMessage**, and the current message transformation logic works on a **per-message basis** — it doesn't have visibility into the full message sequence.

If we apply `.rstrip()` blindly to all AssistantMessages in the transformer stage, it could have unintended side effects, such as:

```python
["show under message\n", "blah, blah"] → ["show under message", "blah, blah"]
```

That’s why I applied the fix after the message list is fully constructed — to avoid over-sanitizing content that’s meant to preserve formatting.

Let me know if you’d prefer a different way to organize this logic!
author: SongChiYoung

body:
(Aside: Why did we originally design the transformer to work per-message?)

That was intentional — based on the **Single Responsibility Principle**.

Message transformers are meant to map the structure of each `LLMMessage` into SDK-specific args (e.g., role, name, content) *in isolation*. They're responsible for how each message "looks" structurally, not how the message sequence should be interpreted as a whole.

In contrast, message stream-level rules — like "strip trailing space from the last AssistantMessage" — depend on *list-level context* and vendor quirks. So they should live in a separate layer like `MessageCleaner`, which operates on the full message sequence.

This keeps responsibilities clear:  
- **Transformer** → adapts message structure  
- **Cleaner** → sanitizes message list

**Orb Code Review** (powered by GLM-4.7 on [Orb Cloud](https://orbcloud.dev))

## Summary

This PR adds a `raw_response` field to the `CreateResult` class to store the original response object returned by model APIs. This addresses issue #6049 by providing a generic way to access custom fields from raw API responses (e.g., `request_id`). The changes span 17 files with 94 total additions and 8 deletions, updating all model clients (Anthropic, Azure, llama.cpp, Ollama, OpenAI, Replay, Semantic Kernel) to populate this field.

## Architecture

**Core Change:**

**File:** `python/packages/autogen-core/src/autogen_core/models/_types.py:146-148`
```python
raw_response: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None
"""Raw response from the model API, useful for custom field access."""
```
- Added optional field to `CreateResult` dataclass
- Type is `Optional[Dict[str, Any]]` (but see type consistency issue below)
- Defaults to `None` for backward compatibility
- Designed to store the full API response object for custom field access

**Model Client Updates:**

All model clients updated to populate `raw_response`:

1. **Anthropic** (`_anthropic_client.py`):
   - `create()`: Passes `result` (Message object)
   - `create_stream()`: Passes `message_result` (Message object)

2. **Azure** (`_azure_ai_client.py`):
   - `create()`: Passes `result`

3. **llama.cpp** (`_llama_cpp_completion_client.py`):
   - `create()`: Passes `response` (dict)
   - Empty response case: Passes `response` (dict)

4. **Ollama** (`_ollama_client.py`):
   - `create()`: Passes `result`
   - `create_stream()`: Passes `None` ⚠️ (inconsistent)

5. **OpenAI** (`_openai_client.py`):
   - `create()`: Passes `result`
   - `create_stream()`: Passes `result`

6. **Replay** (`_replay_chat_completion_client.py`):
   - `create()`: Passes `response` (string)
   - `create_stream()`: Passes `response` (string)

7. **Semantic Kernel** (`_sk_chat_completion_adapter.py`):
   - `create()`: Passes `result`
   - `create_stream()`: Passes `None` ⚠️ (inconsistent)

8. **Chat Completion Client Recorder** (`chat_completion_client_recorder.py`):
   - `create()`: Passes `data.get("raw_response", {"id": "mock-id", "provider": "replay"})`

**Test Updates:**
- All test mocks updated to include `raw_response: {"id": "mock-id", "provider": "replay"}`
- Some test assertion relaxed (test_code_executor_agent.py: check for "SyntaxError" instead of full error string)

**Other Changes:**
- `python/session_1.json`: Modified (appears to be test session data)
- `python/uv.lock`: Dependency lock file updated (15 changes)

## Issues

### Warnings

**_types.py:146** — **Type inconsistency between hint and actual values** — Type hint doesn't match actual types passed:

```python
raw_response: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None  # Type hint says Dict[str, Any]
```

**Actual types passed by clients:**
- Anthropic: `Message` object (from anthropic SDK)
- Azure: Unknown object type
- llama.cpp: `dict`
- Ollama: `dict` (create), `None` (stream)
- OpenAI: `ChatCompletion` object (from openai SDK)
- Replay: `str` (the response content itself)
- Semantic Kernel: Unknown object type (create), `None` (stream)

**Issues:**
- Type hint claims `Dict[str, Any]` but most clients pass SDK objects
- This is misleading and doesn't help users understand what to expect
- Type checkers (mypy) will flag incorrect usages
- IDE autocomplete won't work correctly

**Impact:**
- Users might try to use dict operations on SDK objects
- Type checking will fail in strict environments
- Confusing API contract

**Suggested fix:**
```python
from typing import Any, Optional

raw_response: Optional[Any] = None
"""Raw response from the model API, useful for custom field access.

The type varies by model client:
- Anthropic: anthropic.Message object
- Azure: azure.ai.inference.models.Completions object
- llama.cpp: dict
- Ollama: dict (create) or None (stream)
- OpenAI: openai.types.chat.ChatCompletion object
- Replay: str
- Semantic Kernel: object (create) or None (stream)

Example usage:
    result = await client.create(...)
    request_id = result.raw_response.id if result.raw_response else None
"""
```

**_ollama_client.py:828, _sk_chat_completion_adapter.py:365,373** — **Inconsistent raw_response in streaming** — Streaming methods pass None for raw_response:

```python
# Ollama streaming
async def create_stream(...):
    # ...
    result = CreateResult(
        # ...
        raw_response=None,  # Why None? Non-streaming passes result.
    )

# Semantic Kernel streaming
async def create_stream(...):
    # ...
    result = CreateResult(
        # ...
        raw_response=None,  # Why None? Non-streaming passes result.
    )
```

**Issues:**
- Inconsistent with other clients (OpenAI, Anthropic, llama.cpp, Replay all pass raw response in streaming)
- Users can't access custom fields in streaming responses
- No explanation in comments why these are None
- Makes API harder to use (need to check both `is_streaming` and `raw_response is not None`)

**Impact:**
- Users expecting `raw_response` in streaming will be confused
- Can't access fields like `request_id` in streaming mode
- Inconsistent developer experience across providers

**Suggested fix:**
```python
# Option 1: Populate raw_response in streaming (if available)
async def create_stream(...):
    # ... streaming logic ...
    
    # For Ollama, if you have access to final response:
    if final_response is not None:
        raw_response = final_response
    else:
        raw_response = None
    
    result = CreateResult(
        # ...
        raw_response=raw_response,
    )

# Option 2: Document the limitation clearly
raw_response: Optional[Any] = None
"""Raw response from the model API.

Note: For some providers (Ollama, Semantic Kernel), this may be None in
streaming mode as the complete response object is not available.
"""
```

**_replay_chat_completion_client.py:332,345** — **Passes string instead of response object** — Confusing data type:

```python
response = CreateResult(
    finish_reason="stop",
    content=response,  # This is the string content
    usage=self._cur_usage,
    cached=self._cached_bool_value,
    raw_response=response,  # Same string? Should be the full response object.
)
```

**Issues:**
- Both `content` and `raw_response` are set to the same string value
- `raw_response` should contain the full response object, not just the content string
- Doesn't match the pattern used by other clients
- Makes `raw_response` useless for this client

**Suggested fix:**
```python
# If the replay client has access to full response structure:
response = CreateResult(
    finish_reason="stop",
    content=response_text,
    usage=self._cur_usage,
    cached=self._cached_bool_value,
    raw_response={
        "content": response_text,
        "finish_reason": "stop",
        "usage": self._cur_usage.dict(),
        "cached": self._cached_bool_value,
    },
)

# Or if only content is available, make it clear:
raw_response={"content": response_text},
```

**session_1.json** — **Unintended file modification** — Local test file included in PR:

**File:** `python/session_1.json`
**Changes:** 24 additions, 0 deletions

**Issue:**
- This appears to be a local test session or cache file
- Should not be committed to the repository
- May contain sensitive or temporary test data
- Usually found in `.gitignore` for Python projects

**Suggested fix:**
1. **Remove the file from the PR** if it shouldn't be tracked:
```bash
git rm --cached python/session_1.json
echo "python/session_1.json" >> .gitignore
```

2. **OR explain** why this file needs to be tracked in the PR description

**No usage examples or documentation** — Users don't know how to use raw_response:

**Issue:**
- PR description is minimal (1 sentence)
- No examples of how to access `request_id` or other fields
- No documentation of what fields are available for each provider
- No warning about type variations

**Impact:**
- Users will be confused about how to use this feature
- Trial-and-error required to figure out available fields
- High risk of misuse or errors

**Suggested fix:**
Add comprehensive documentation:
```python
raw_response: Optional[Any] = None
"""Raw response from the model API, useful for custom field access.

This field contains the complete response object from the underlying model API,
allowing access to provider-specific fields not exposed in the standard CreateResult.

Common use cases:
- Accessing request/response IDs for debugging or tracing
- Retrieving provider-specific metadata (e.g., model version, region)
- Logging full API responses for audit purposes

Examples:

    # Access OpenAI request ID
    result = await client.create(...)
    if result.raw_response:
        request_id = result.raw_response.id  # OpenAI ChatCompletion object
        print(f"Request ID: {request_id}")

    # Access Anthropic usage details
    result = await client.create(...)
    if result.raw_response:
        usage = result.raw_response.usage  # Anthropic Message object
        print(f"Total tokens: {usage.input_tokens + usage.output_tokens}")

    # Access Ollama model details
    result = await client.create(...)
    if result.raw_response:
        model = result.raw_response.get("model", "unknown")
        print(f"Model: {model}")

Provider-specific types:
- Anthropic: anthropic.Message (see https://docs.anthropic.com/)
- Azure: azure.ai.inference.models.Completions (see Azure docs)
- llama.cpp: dict with response data
- Ollama: dict (see https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md)
- OpenAI: openai.types.chat.ChatCompletion (see https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference)
- Replay: dict with mock data
- Semantic Kernel: varies by model

Note: The structure and available fields vary by provider and API version.
Always check for None before accessing fields.
"""
```

### Suggestions

**Add serialization support** for CreateResult with raw_response:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator

class CreateResult(BaseModel):
    # ... existing fields ...
    raw_response: Optional[Any] = Field(default=None, exclude=True)
    """Raw response from the model API. Excluded from JSON serialization."""
    
    @field_validator('raw_response', mode='before')
    @classmethod
    def make_serializable(cls, v: Any) -> Any:
        """Attempt to make raw_response JSON-serializable."""
        if v is None:
            return None
        
        # If it's already a dict, return as-is
        if isinstance(v, dict):
            return v
        
        # If it has a model_dump method (Pydantic models), use it
        if hasattr(v, 'model_dump'):
            return v.model_dump()
        
        # If it has a dict method, use it
        if hasattr(v, 'dict'):
            return v.dict()
        
        # If it's a string, wrap in dict
        if isinstance(v, str):
            return {"content": v}
        
        # Otherwise, convert to string and wrap
        return {"raw": str(v)}
```

**Add helper methods** for common raw_response operations:

```python
class CreateResult(BaseModel):
    # ... existing fields ...
    raw_response: Optional[Any] = None
    
    def get_raw_field(self, field_name: str, default: Any = None) -> Any:
        """Safely get a field from raw_response.
        
        Handles both dict and object access patterns.
        
        Args:
            field_name: Name of the field to retrieve
            default: Default value if field not found
            
        Returns:
            Field value or default
            
        Example:
            result = await client.create(...)
            request_id = result.get_raw_field("id", "unknown")
        """
        if self.raw_response is None:
            return default
        
        # Try dict access first
        if isinstance(self.raw_response, dict):
            return self.raw_response.get(field_name, default)
        
        # Try attribute access
        if hasattr(self.raw_response, field_name):
            return getattr(self.raw_response, field_name)
        
        return default
    
    def has_raw_field(self, field_name: str) -> bool:
        """Check if raw_response has a specific field.
        
        Args:
            field_name: Name of the field to check
            
        Returns:
            True if field exists, False otherwise
        """
        if self.raw_response is None:
            return False
        
        if isinstance(self.raw_response, dict):
            return field_name in self.raw_response
        
        return hasattr(self.raw_response, field_name)
```

**Add validation** for raw_response in tests:

```python
# tests/test_raw_response.py
import pytest
from autogen_core.models import CreateResult, RequestUsage

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_raw_response_dict_access():

    result = CreateResult(

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_raw_response_none_safety():
    """Test safe access when raw_response is None."""
    result = CreateResult(
        content="Hello",

        raw_response=None,
    )
    
    assert result.get_raw_field("id", "default") == "default"
    assert not result.has_raw_field("id")
```

```python
class CreateResult(BaseModel):
    # ... existing fields ...
    raw_response: Optional[Any] = None
    
    def get_openai_request_id(self) -> Optional[str]:

```

**Add memory usage consideration** in documentation:

```python
raw_response: Optional[Any] = None
"""Raw response from the model API.

Note: This field stores the complete API response object, which may
include large amounts of data (e.g., full prompt, all choices, logprobs).
For memory-constrained environments or long-running applications, consider
processing the required fields immediately and setting raw_response to None
if not needed.

Example:
    result = await client.create(...)
    # Extract needed fields immediately
    request_id = result.get_raw_field("id")
    usage = result.usage
    # Clear raw_response to free memory
    result.raw_response = None
"""

Warning: The structure and available fields in raw_response may change

    result = await client.create(...)

## Cross-file Impact

**Modified Files (17 total):**

**Core Type Definition:**
- `python/packages/autogen-core/src/autogen_core/models/_types.py` — Added raw_response field (4 additions, 1 deletion)

**Model Client Implementations:**
- `python/packages/autogen-ext/src/autogen_ext/models/anthropic/_anthropic_client.py` — Populate raw_response (8 additions)
- `python/packages/autogen-ext/src/autogen_ext/models/azure/_azure_ai_client.py` — Populate raw_response (1 addition)

- `python/packages/autogen-ext/tests/test_openai_assistant_agent.py` — Add raw_response to mocks (8 additions)

**Other:**
- `python/session_1.json` — Unintended file modification (24 additions) ⚠️
- `python/uv.lock` — Dependency lock file updates (3 additions, 12 deletions)

**Dependencies:**
- No new dependencies added
- uv.lock updated (likely due to test data changes)

**Breaking Changes:**
- None - backward compatible (new optional field with default None)

**Public API:**
- `CreateResult.raw_response` — New optional field
- Type: `Optional[Dict[str, Any]]` (but actual types vary)
- Default: `None`

**Test Coverage:**
- Existing tests updated to include `raw_response` in mock data
- No new tests specifically for `raw_response` functionality
- **Missing**: Tests for accessing raw_response fields, type validation, serialization

**Documentation:**

- Docstring added to field (brief)
- **Missing**: Usage examples, provider-specific field documentation, type variations explanation

**User Impact:**
- Users can now access custom API response fields (e.g., `request_id`)
- **Potential confusion**: Type hint doesn't match actual types
- **Inconsistency**: Some streaming clients don't populate raw_response
- **No guidance**: Users must figure out field names through trial-and-error

**Performance:**
- Minimal performance impact
- Storing full API response increases memory usage slightly
- No runtime overhead when `raw_response=None`

**Compatibility:**
- Backward compatible (new optional field)
- Forward compatible (existing code unaffected)
- Type inconsistency may cause issues with type checkers

## Assessment

⚠️ Request changes

This PR adds valuable functionality but has several issues that should be addressed before merge:

**Critical Issues:**
1. **Type inconsistency**: Type hint claims `Dict[str, Any]` but most clients pass SDK objects, misleading users and breaking type checking.

2. **Streaming inconsistency**: Ollama and Semantic Kernel pass `None` for `raw_response` in streaming mode, while other providers pass the full response object.

3. **Unintended file**: `python/session_1.json` appears to be a local test file that shouldn't be in the PR.

**Why Request Changes:**

1. **Type safety**: The incorrect type hint will cause type checkers to flag errors and confuse users about what to expect.

2. **API consistency**: Users expect `raw_response` to be available in all cases, but streaming mode is inconsistent.

3. **Code quality**: Including unintended local files in PRs is poor practice and may contain sensitive data.

**Required Changes Before Approval:**

1. **Fix type hint**:
   - Change `Optional[Dict[str, Any]]` to `Optional[Any]`
   - Add comprehensive docstring explaining type variations by provider
   - Document what fields are commonly available for each provider

2. **Address streaming inconsistency**:
   - Either populate `raw_response` in streaming (if data available) OR
   - Document clearly which providers don't support it in streaming mode

3. **Fix unintended file**:
   - Remove `python/session_1.json` from the PR
   - Add to `.gitignore` if it shouldn't be tracked

4. **Fix Replay client**:
   - Pass a proper response object (dict) instead of just the content string

5. **Add documentation**:
   - Include usage examples in docstring
   - Document common use cases (accessing `request_id`, etc.)
   - Add warnings about type variations and version compatibility

6. **Add helper methods** (optional but recommended):
   - `get_raw_field(field_name, default)` for safe field access
   - `has_raw_field(field_name)` for checking field existence
   - Provider-specific accessors (e.g., `get_openai_request_id()`)

**Positive Aspects:**
- Addresses a real user need (issue #6049)
- Backward compatible design
- Comprehensive test updates (all existing tests updated)
- Consistent pattern across most model clients
- Minimal code changes for maximum benefit
- Good use of optional field for backward compatibility

**Recommendation:**
This PR has the right idea and implementation is mostly good, but the type inconsistency, streaming inconsistency, and unintended file need to be addressed before merge. The changes are relatively simple:

1. Update type hint and add comprehensive documentation
2. Fix or document streaming inconsistencies
3. Remove unintended file
4. Fix Replay client implementation

With these changes, this PR will provide valuable functionality with a clean, well-documented API.

Hi @abhinav-aegis ,

Thanks for putting this together, much appreciated. I am personally excited to see this take shape and ideally, it would be great to see it get to a point where we support it in AutoGen Studio. 

That said, as we improve it, what is a good **minimum testable example** we can use to help readers of this thread get a good sense of what is being accomplished. Will also provide some framework for expected behaviour. 

Perhaps something like the below (B and C below seem to not be responding with )?

```python

from autogen_ext.models.openai._openai_client import OpenAIChatCompletionClient
from autogen_ext.models.openai._openai_client import OpenAIChatCompletionClient
from autogen_agentchat.agents import (
    AssistantAgent,
)
from autogen_agentchat.conditions import MaxMessageTermination
from autogen_agentchat.teams._group_chat._digraph_group_chat import DiGraphGroupChat, DiGraph, DiGraphNode, DiGraphEdge 


model_client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(model="gpt-4o-mini")
agent_a = AssistantAgent("A", model_client=model_client, system_message="You are a helpful assistant.")
agent_b = AssistantAgent("B", model_client=model_client, system_message="You are a helpful spanish translator. Whenever you receive a message, translate it to Spanish and respond with the translation.")
agent_c = AssistantAgent("C", model_client=model_client, system_message="You are a helpful assistant markdown assistant. Whenever you receieve a message format it as markdown (use tables where appropriate) and respond with the formatted message.")

graph = DiGraph(
    nodes={
        "A": DiGraphNode(name="A", edges=[DiGraphEdge(target="B")]),
        "B": DiGraphNode(name="B", edges=[DiGraphEdge(target="C")]),
        "C": DiGraphNode(name="C", edges=[]),
    }
)

team = DiGraphGroupChat(
    participants=[agent_a, agent_b, agent_c],
    graph=graph,
    termination_condition=MaxMessageTermination(5),
)
 
stream =  team.run_stream(task="Write a 3 line haiku poem about the amount of rainfail each month for california.")
async for message in stream:
    print("********",message) 

```

Result 

```python
TaskResult(messages=[TextMessage(source='user', models_usage=None, metadata={}, content='Write a 3 line haiku poem about the amount of rainfail each month for california.', type='TextMessage'), TextMessage(source='A', models_usage=RequestUsage(prompt_tokens=37, completion_tokens=21), metadata={}, content="Winter's soft whispers,  \nSpring's vibrant blooms drink deeply,  \nSummer's drought holds sway.", type='TextMessage'), TextMessage(source='B', models_usage=RequestUsage(prompt_tokens=79, completion_tokens=27), metadata={}, content='Susurros de invierno,  \nLas flores vibrantes de primavera beben profundamente,  \nLa sequía del verano prevalece.', type='TextMessage'), TextMessage(source='C', models_usage=RequestUsage(prompt_tokens=118, completion_tokens=64), metadata={}, content="### Haiku about California Rainfall\n\n**English:**\n\nWinter's soft whispers,  \nSpring's vibrant blooms drink deeply,  \nSummer's drought holds sway.\n\n---\n\n**Spanish:**\n\nSusurros de invierno,  \nLas flores vibrantes de primavera beben profundamente,  \nLa sequía del verano prevalece.", type='TextMessage')], stop_reason='The DiGraph chat has finished executing.')
```

Really interesting PoC

especially the memory integration and the use of `difflib` for comparison, that part caught my eye.

One idea that came to mind: what if the message were internally stored as structured JSON, and only rendered into Markdown at the final presentation stage?

There are probably existing libraries that can help with this, or if not, I'd be happy to explore writing a lightweight one. I feel like this could enable more precise edit control (e.g., asking the LLM to rewrite only a specific field) and make the entire revision flow more composable.

Would love to hear what you think!

body:
Thanks @lspinheiro 
here's a rough draft of what I had in mind.

Suppose we have Markdown like this:

```markdown
# Hello world
## My name 
* Song Chi Young 
* a.k.a EeS
```

We could internally represent it as JSON like (Just DRAFT):
```json
{
  "type": "h1",
  "context": ["Hello world"],
  "inner": [
    {
      "type": "h2",
      "context": ["My name"],
      "inner": [
        {
          "type": "list",
          "context": [
            "Song Chi Young",
            "a.k.a EeS"
          ],
          "inner": []
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

This structure uses a simple schema like:
```json
{
  "type": "<markdown block type>",
  "context": ["<text contents>"],
  "inner": [<nested blocks>]
}
```

And yes — you’re absolutely right: LLMs understand Markdown much better than raw JSON.
So the idea is: when editing, we don’t send the JSON to the LLM 

we **extract just the relevant block**, convert it to Markdown, and prompt the LLM with that.

Example:
```python
# Convert JSON to markdown block
markdown_block = render_to_markdown(target_json_block)

# Send only that to LLM
send_to_llm(markdown_block)
```

target_json_block
```json
{
    "type": "h2",
    "context": ["My name"],
    "inner": [
      {
        "type": "list",
        "context": [
          "Song Chi Young",
          "a.k.a EeS"
        ],
        "inner": []
      }
    ]
}
```
markdown_block
```markdown
## My name 
* Song Chi Young 
* a.k.a EeS
```

Then after receiving the modified Markdown, we parse it back into JSON and store it in that form.

I think this approach could make Canvas block editing more modular, traceable, and LLM-friendly.
Would love to hear your thoughts!


---

Now that I think about it, we’re really just managing it as a Python dict, not necessarily JSON.
But I do think keeping the JSON structure in mind is still important
especially when it comes to serialization or portability.


The key idea here is to manage Markdown in a Pythonic way — breaking it into composable, addressable blocks that we can send and receive individually.

> ```
> # Hello world
> ## My name 
> * Song Chi Young 
> * a.k.a EeS
> ```
> 
> We could internally represent it as JSON like (Just DRAFT):
> 
> ```json
> {
>   "type": "h1",
>   "context": ["Hello world"],
>   "inner": [
>     {
>       "type": "h2",
>       "context": ["My name"],
>       "inner": [
>         {
>           "type": "list",
>           "context": [
>             "Song Chi Young",
>             "a.k.a EeS"
>           ],
>           "inner": []
>         }
>       ]
>     }
>   ]
> }
> ```
> 
> This structure uses a simple schema like:
> 
> ```json
> {
>   "type": "<markdown block type>",
>   "context": ["<text contents>"],
>   "inner": [<nested blocks>]
> }
> ```
> 
> And yes — you’re absolutely right: LLMs understand Markdown much better than raw JSON. So the idea is: when editing, we don’t send the JSON to the LLM
> 
> we **extract just the relevant block**, convert it to Markdown, and prompt the LLM with that.
> 
> Example:
> 
> ```python
> # Convert JSON to markdown block
> markdown_block = render_to_markdown(target_json_block)
> 
> # Send only that to LLM
> send_to_llm(markdown_block)
> ```
> 
> target_json_block
> 
> ```json
> {
>     "type": "h2",
>     "context": ["My name"],
>     "inner": [
>       {
>         "type": "list",
>         "context": [
>           "Song Chi Young",
>           "a.k.a EeS"
>         ],
>         "inner": []
>       }
>     ]
> }
> ```
> 
> markdown_block
> 
> ```
> ## My name 
> * Song Chi Young 
> * a.k.a EeS
> ```
> 
> Then after receiving the modified Markdown, we parse it back into JSON and store it in that form.
> 
> I think this approach could make Canvas block editing more modular, traceable, and LLM-friendly. Would love to hear your thoughts!
> 
> Now that I think about it, we’re really just managing it as a Python dict, not necessarily JSON. But I do think keeping the JSON structure in mind is still important especially when it comes to serialization or portability.
> 
> The key idea here is to manage Markdown in a Pythonic way — breaking it into composable, addressable blocks that we can send and receive individually.

Would you have an application that could exemplify how this format would be helpful? The current implementation is based on the assumption that the canvas is a store for file-like objects with revisions. I probably didnt explain it well but even for the markdown, that is not an assumed format, it is more like a text file which could be markdown, a code file (e.g. *.py), etc. Then, what we do is calculate the text-diff.

the objective is to be able to present the revisions of the file in something like autogen-studio, similar to how we can do in Claude (I haven't used much either Gemini or ChatGPT canvas but I assume it works in a similar way).

So, based on this, I'm not sure if a json-like structure would be that helpful for general documents. I think we can use it for some types of outputs that use structured outputs because I think there are some specialized json-diff tools that could be helpful. Does that make sense?

That being said, I think the current Canvas/FileRevision classes could use an improved design where we consider extension to different types of files, diff-algorithms, storage, distributed access, etc.
author: lspinheiro

body:
Lately, I’ve been exploring ways to use AutoGen to build a more effective version of DeepResearch — especially in how we generate and revise long-form documents in a modular and scalable way.

That’s where I believe a structured block representation of document content can be useful.

As you pointed out, for code files, a single block like `{type: "python", content: <source_code>}` may be enough — and in such cases, the benefits of deeper structure may be limited. Still, using a consistent structural format provides value: it clarifies file types, improves modularity, and supports extensibility even if the content itself is flat.

> Even for non-Markdown formats, we could fall back on tools like `difflib` to compute revisions, while maintaining structured metadata in parallel.

From what I’ve observed, LLM-based tools like Claude and ChatGPT appear to operate on block-level edits — particularly in report-style contexts. While we don’t know their exact internal mechanisms, the UX suggests chunk-level interaction and partial rewrites are common, and I believe this can inform how we approach scalable document editing.

Now, if the document isn't code or Markdown — just unstructured prose — what should we do?

The most robust solution, I think, is to enforce Markdown formatting via prompting. In fact, many existing systems seem to do this, or even push further into structured JSON outputs (e.g., tool/function calls). As a fallback, we could chunk based on paragraph boundaries (e.g., double line breaks), but practically speaking — if we're dealing with general-purpose documents, it's unclear why we *wouldn't* want to treat Markdown as the default.

So instead of modifying the core canvas abstraction, my suggestion is to represent each file revision as a `dict`-style object composed of typed blocks, and use prompting to standardize Markdown output when interacting with LLMs.

This approach provides structure, simplifies partial editing, and scales better as document complexity increases. It also brings consistency across file types — whether it's code, markdown, or anything else — while staying aligned with how LLMs seem to internally manage long-form content.

---

Building on this, I think the Tool interface could expose additional capabilities:

- Return just the structural layout (e.g., headings, nesting)  
- Or: return full content up to a certain depth, and structure-only beyond that

This could significantly reduce token usage, and help LLMs request only the chunks they actually need — making non-contiguous edits and multi-agent collaboration across a single document more feasible.

In short, exposing both structure and content in a composable way gives the LLM the ability to reason about *where* and *how* to make changes, without needing to ingest the entire file at once.

If it sounds interesting, I’d be happy to explore a small prototype on top of your current design — just as an experiment to see how it might fit.
